title: Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
description: Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise
fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church's latest show of support for President ‌Vladimir Putin's war.

The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at ‌the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow's Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.

Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince's well-preserved remains in August, hailing them ​as "an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery" which reinforced the foundations of Russian history.

The Russian Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy's right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Putin said he had incorporated into Russia in 2022, a move Kyiv rejected as an illegal land grab.

Referring to Donskoy as "the holy commander," the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russian Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russian troops.

"A fragment of the ‌Grand Prince's right hand – the very same right hand with ⁠which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field – has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers' spirits," it said in a statement.

The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russian combat units along the more than 1,000-km ⁠front line, it said.

Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War Two, was declared a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988.

The carefully choreographed effort to use his remains in a public relations exercise to boost patriotism and morale comes ahead of a parliamentary election later this month.

Russian military and church officials have ​presented ​the discovery as a fortuitous find that could help Russian forces prevail in Ukraine, now in ​the fifth year of a grinding war.

The tour also comes as ‌Russian forces seek full control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and as diplomatic efforts to end the war have yet to yield a breakthrough.

Donskoy's relics were carried through the streets of Moscow at the weekend in a huge Orthodox procession.

At a ceremony at a World War Two memorial in Donetsk on Tuesday, Sergei Kiriyenko, Putin's first deputy Kremlin chief of staff, joined military commanders and the Russian-installed regional head in kissing the relic and making the sign of the cross as a priest read a prayer.

"Both our military personnel and the people who live in Donbas need strengthening from above, need God's help and the blessing of our saints," Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol, a senior Moscow-appointed ‌cleric, said. Donbas is a broader area incorporating Donetsk and neighbouring Luhansk which Russia controls almost in ​its entirety.

Elsewhere, commanders have presented Donskoy's remains as evidence that God is on Russia's side.

The Defence Ministry ​on Wednesday released footage of troops in the Sverdlovsk region attending a church ​service carrying icons and Orthodox flags, alongside an interview with a commander who said the relics would support Russia's victory.

Critics, however, have accused ‌the Church of breaking with religious protocol to please the Kremlin. ​They have also questioned why Donskoy's remains, whose ​location was broadly known for decades, were recovered and venerated only now, 38 years after he was declared a saint.

"By the fifth year of war, the Church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its 'special military operation'," Alexander Zanemonets, an ​Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, wrote in a note ‌for the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center whose director Russia has designated a "foreign agent."

"It had already sent priests to the front lines, instituted mandatory prayers ​for Russian victory in every church, and flown icons over cities. A state embroiled in war will try to compel all institutions, including religious ​ones, to participate in it."

title: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia’s Arctic gas heartland as Trump pushes Putin toward peace
description: Ukrainian drones struck Novy Urengoy, sparking a fire in Russia's top natural-gas region roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border in the Arctic.
fullText:
Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia's Arctic north Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia's most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and the Associated Press.

Regional Gov. Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site. He did not identify the facility, and the extent of the damage was still being assessed, Reuters reported Wednesday.

Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting: "Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target."

The extraordinary strike comes as Washington makes a renewed push to end the more than four-year war even as Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on each other.

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had just spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both Moscow and Kyiv may be prepared to negotiate.

"We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice," Trump said.

Asked what was holding up an agreement, Trump pointed to the personal animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling them "two people that hate each other."

"These are two people that are tired of fighting," Trump added.

Trump's comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive negotiations. The talks produced no breakthrough, according to the Associated Press.

Russian Strikes Continue Following Visit By Witkoff And Kushner To Kyiv

Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left Ukraine, killing five people and wounding 35 on Tuesday, Reuters reported.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a long-standing dilemma for Western governments trying to engage Moscow.

"You have to talk, you have to explain," the source said, arguing that communication is necessary to prevent misunderstandings.

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

But the source said Russian officials can interpret Western outreach differently.

"Whenever you talk with them, they consider that this is a Western weakness," the source said, adding that the assessment was based in part on informal contacts with Russian officials.

The source also said Putin's recent emphasis on Russian "military progress in Ukraine" appeared aimed in part at Washington, projecting strength as U.S. officials seek to revive negotiations.

The escalation is taking an increasing toll on civilians. The United Nations said last month that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded.

More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its strikes are aimed at military and military-related facilities.

Drone Offensive Hits Russian Oil Tankers And Refineries At 'Industrial Scale' As Moscow Bans Diesel Exports

United24 described Wednesday's attack as the deepest Ukrainian drone strike inside Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Novy Urengoy lies roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border. Artem Zhoga, Putin's envoy to Russia's Urals Federal District, said a Ukrainian drone had attempted to strike a fuel-and-energy facility in Yamal, according to Meduza.

The city sits in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, the country's dominant natural-gas producing region. About 80% of Russia's natural gas is extracted there, according to Interfax data cited by the Associated Press.

Artyukhov said there were no reported casualties.

The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault on Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck targets around the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, including a naval base, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships capable of carrying cruise missiles, according to the Associated Press.

Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in the Novorossiysk attack.

Russia, meanwhile, continued its own long-range campaign against Ukraine Wednesday. Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while another wave of attacks on Kyiv killed one person and wounded 14, according to Reuters.

description: Ukraine's national motorsport authority calls on FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem to impose sanctions on its Russian counterpart for opening offices in occupied parts of Ukraine.
fullText:
Ukraine's national motorsport authority has called on FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem to impose sanctions on its Russian counterpart.

The Russian automobile federation has opened offices in occupied parts of Ukraine in violation of the rules of the FIA, motorsport's governing body, according to the Ukraine federation (FAU).

The offices in Crimea, the city of Sevastopol and the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts are all located in areas recognised as sovereign Ukrainian territory by the United Nations.

The FAU's appeal for sanctions against its Russian counterpart (RAF) is the latest step it has made following the FIA's decision last month to lift the ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors in motorsport.

The FAU said in a statement that it was "outraged by the prolonged inaction of the global governing body".

It added: "The FAU has already appealed to the FIA senate and FIA ethics committee, but has received no reaction or reply."

It has also lodged a case with the FIA's international court of appeal.

FAU president Oleksander Feldman has written to Ben Sulayem demanding action.

He wrote: "Such short-sighted and counterproductive inaction is unbecoming of representatives of a global governing body. The current situation could have catastrophic consequences for the FIA's global standing.

"This is a dangerous precedent that paves the way for member organisations to disregard other provisions of the statutes and requirements of the rules, potentially leading to chaos and jeopardising the FIA's future as an institution."

Ukraine escalates protest over FIA lifting Russia ban

The FIA's rules permit only one automobile club or national sporting authority per country.

Feldman's letter demands that Ben Sulayem suspends Russia's membership, re-imposes "strict restrictions on Russian athletes' participation in international competitions", and makes a statement that publicly declares, on behalf of the FIA, that "the forcible redistribution of sporting authority is unacceptable".

The letter comes a week after Ukraine's minister for youth and sport told BBC Sport the FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors.

Matvii Bidnyi said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

"Russia continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Belarus continues to provide military support to Russia. Ukrainian people are still being killed every day. And Russian attacks become more and more brutal.

"I don't understand, and Ukrainian people and I know that all European people don't understand what's happened, why now we must make this policy softer."

The ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors taking part in international motorsport events was imposed in February 2022, after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine.

It was lifted on 3 August in a decision by the FIA's world motorsport council. This followed the International Olympic Committee, with which the FIA is affiliated, lifting its own ban.

Other sporting authorities, such as World Athletics, have not followed suit.

The Russian Embassy in London said in a statement to BBC Sport last week: "Excluding Russian athletes from international competitions amounts to segregation based on nationality and is incompatible with the principles of the Olympic charter.

"The FIA's decision to lift the restrictions on Russian competitors in international motorsport is a step in the right direction. It shows that common sense is gradually prevailing over political bias in major sporting federations."

The FIA has been contacted for comment.

title: Germany to send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine, warns of stepped-up Russian winter attacks

fullText:
Sept 8 (Reuters) - Germany will send Patriot air defence missiles to Ukraine from its national stocks, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on ‌Tuesday, warning that Russia was likely to intensify its air campaign ‌against Ukrainian infrastructure as winter approaches.

Speaking at a videoconference of nations supporting Ukraine, Pistorius said ​he had decided to "deliver urgently" additional PAC-2 interceptor missiles.

Patriot missiles are currently the only effective defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine, officials say.

"Since Russia is only advancing very slowly at the front line, it is trying to destroy ‌Ukraine's economic base and ⁠critical infrastructure by way of air raids on port installations, power plants, and other civilian targets," Pistorius said.

"Unfortunately, we can ⁠expect Russian air raids to increase again once temperatures drop, and then the damage will be even greater," he told the meeting of the Ukraine Defence ​Contact ​Group.

Pistorius did not say how many missiles ​Germany would provide.

He said Germany ‌would also expand deliveries of air-to-air missiles and continue supplying drones and long-range ammunition to Kyiv.

Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Kyiv is contracting to buy around 1,000 Patriot missiles but most would only be shipped in the coming years. He urged allies to dig into their stocks for ‌Ukraine now, on the basis that Kyiv would ​replace those missiles from future deliveries.

NATO Secretary ​General Mark Rutte also pressed ​allies to increase support, saying civilian casualties from the ‌war were at their highest level since ​May 2022.

"Nations must ​dig deeper. We do not have a choice," he said.

Ahead of the meeting, Rutte and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said ​EU members states ‌had agreed to use part of a €90-billion ($105 billion) EU loan to ​allow Ukraine to buy crucial supplies for Patriot systems.

title: Ukraine prosecutor general resigns in latest fallout from anti-corruption crackdown

fullText:
KYIV, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's prosecutor general resigned his post late on Monday after a corruption investigation reached his office, becoming the latest senior official ensnared in an ‌intensified anti-graft crackdown by Kyiv's independent watchdogs.

Ruslan Kravchenko was not charged with a crime or named ‌a suspect in any investigation. But authorities had accused a subordinate of helping run a fraud ring, prompting the presidential appointee to ​quit to avoid "political confrontation".

"This is a political decision, and I have made it consciously," said Kravchenko, 36, in a statement. He denied any wrongdoing.

The case is the latest in a series of high-profile corruption scandals that have claimed the jobs of senior officials in President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's government and forced several wartime shake-ups.

Zelenskiy said on Tuesday he ‌would submit Kravchenko's request to parliament, ⁠where lawmakers must approve his resignation.

The investigation by the NABU and SAPO agencies, announced on Saturday, centres on a department manager whom prosecutors say took bribes ⁠for helping to cover up a call centre that defrauded Ukrainians and foreigners.

They said the official recruited fellow employees and friends to launder nearly $1 million in proceeds through real estate purchases and other assets.

The agencies published photos of a ​safe ​filled with stacks of cash and detectives confiscating a luxury ​SUV.

Such vivid instances of alleged graft have ‌fuelled public anger at a time when Ukraine is fighting for survival against Russia.

Last year, Zelenskiy faced the worst political crisis of the war after his ex-business partner was accused of running a $100 million kickback scheme at the state atomic agency.

CALLS TO REFORM PROSECUTOR'S OFFICE

Kravchenko had been criticised by opponents for allegedly participating in an attempt to roll back the powers of NABU and SAPO last year - accusations he has denied.

In Ukraine, the ‌prosecutor's office enjoys considerable powers, ranging from probing corruption to ​investigating war crimes.

Zelenskiy, who had faced protests last year over ​the proposed restrictions on the anti-corruption agencies, said ​on Tuesday that he had met with Kravchenko as well as NABU and SAPO ‌following the latest investigation.

Opposition lawmaker Andrii Osadchuk, deputy ​chair of parliament's law-enforcement committee, ​said the scandal underlines the need to reform the prosecution service and called for key posts to be filled through open competition.

Fighting corruption is also critical to Kyiv's bid for membership in ​the European Union.

"It will be very ‌difficult for Ukraine to move forward if we do not change the approach to selecting and ​appointing the prosecutor general and prosecutors at lower levels," Osadchuk said.

(Additional reporting by Jekaterīna Golubkova ​in Tokyo; Editing by Stephen Coates and Ros Russell)

fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 8 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday in a phone call that ‌he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, ‌something that would allow U.S.-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said.

Kremlin aide ​Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the pair had discussed the outcome of U.S. peace negotiators' weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv - something he said both leaders had rated "with a plus sign" - and said that Putin had ‌told Trump what he ⁠believed the United States could do to help end the conflict.

Putin had also given Trump his assessment of what ⁠the situation on the battlefield was and had made it clear that Russia had no hostile plans towards Europe, Ushakov said.

"Donald Trump clearly emphasised the ​desirability of ​bringing the conflict to an ​end as soon as possible, ‌which would immediately open up prospects – impressive and far-reaching ones at that – for the full restoration of relations between the U.S. and Russia," said Ushakov.

"In his view, this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries. Donald Trump ‌is keen to see a breakthrough ​achieved during his presidency. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin ​supported this approach".

Ushakov - who said ​Putin and Trump had also agreed on the ‌need to continue prisoner exchanges - said he ​was not able ​to get into more details about what had been discussed, but described the conversation as constructive and said the two leaders had ​agreed they would stay ‌in touch and speak to each other by phone again ​if the needed arose.

title: Ukraine's front lines are so dangerous that troops take casualties just moving in and out of their own trenches
description: Ukraine's drone-filled front lines have made even routine movement in and out of trenches a deadly risk for troops.
fullText:
Ukrainian troops often take casualties moving in and out of trenches, a Western commander said.

Drones and other weapons make even routine movement near the front extremely dangerous.

The threat can leave soldiers stuck in defensive positions for days or even longer.

Ukraine's front lines are unforgivingly brutal, and soldiers are often injured or killed just rotating in and out of their own trench systems, a Western commander leading a training program for Ukrainian soldiers told Business Insider.

"We hear that Ukrainian forces take quite a few casualties infiltrating and exfiltrating out of their own trench systems because the front has been static for a very long time," said Brigadier Atle Molde, the commander of Task Force Legio, a Norway-led multinational effort to train Ukrainian soldiers on NATO soil.

Swarms of drones overhead gather intelligence and attack, making any movement a risk. Ukrainian commanders have described troop rotations as among the most vulnerable moments for front-line soldiers.

The drone-saturated area around the front lines is often described as a "kill zone." A Ukrainian official previously told Business Insider that just getting to front-line positions can take days and that it is the most dangerous part of the mission in many cases.

Troop rotation, resupply, and relocation also present tremendous risks.

That danger is why the Western training program puts particular emphasis on moving in and out of trench systems. At Camp Jomsborg, a purpose-built training site in eastern Poland, "it's all about saving lives," Molde said.

Jørgen, a Norwegian Army instructor for the operation's platoon leader course who spoke on the condition that only his first name be used, told Business Insider that the training includes using supporting fire to suppress the enemy so that friendly forces can move into trenches.

He said that many of the Ukrainians who come through already have an "incredibly high" level of combat experience and have developed effective methods of their own. The input he has received from Ukrainian trainees "worked when I actually tried to do it," he shared, and resulted in "less risk to our guys."

Trenches have long been surrounded by death and difficulty in this war. Worsening threats, particularly the drone threat, however, have at times made this situation significantly more dangerous.

Soldiers can get stuck inside trenches, dugouts, and other defensive positions for long periods.

Some troops have described having to spend months in a single position because drones and artillery made it too dangerous to move out safely. They had to wait for weather, friendly fire support, or a lucky break to move without immediately being detected and attacked.

A US veteran who fought for Ukraine previously told Business Insider that life in a trench was often just waiting as "artillery shells just dropping on you for hours on end," they said.

The danger can make seemingly basic tasks difficult. The veteran said troops couldn't even properly remove enemy dead, while another American vet who fought for Ukraine said that soldiers sometimes struggled to deepen or fortify their trenches because they didn't want to "stick their heads out."

"When guys have tried to move," the veteran said, "they step out and immediately just start getting pounded, and then they're having to play dead, hoping that eventually they'll catch a quick break to get up and start running."

Even staying put can offer little security. They described being "literally just hunkered down" and hoping nothing collapsed the position or landed inside the trench. "You're static in one spot, and there's not much you can do about it."

When troops can't safely rotate in and out, soldiers can end up stranded at the front for long periods.

Soldiers from Ukraine's 121st Territorial Brigade said in August that they had gone four months without a rotation and were running short of food and water, the Kyiv Independent reported at the time.

Command said that they would be pulled out when the security situation allowed. Heavy drone surveillance had made movement to and from forward positions difficult.

At Camp Jomsborg, Ukrainian combat experience, including its deep knowledge of trench warfare, is being combined with Western best practices and incorporated into how troops train to move through and fight from trenches.

Jørgen said the trench infiltration and exfiltration tactics the Ukrainians had shown him were better than any single lesson he had to offer. "Keeping it to the principles and trying to let the guys put their own experience into it," he said, "I think that's much more valuable than my experience."

The trench warfare in Ukraine is unlike anything Western militaries have seen in a long time. Positions are watched by drones, the battlefield kill chains are faster, allowing movement to be detected and engaged in minutes, and even routine supply runs and rotations can become deadly combat operations.

The West is paying attention and, through work with the Ukrainians, reassessing its training and assumptions about this kind of warfighting.

At Camp Jomsborg, leaders are trying to get the trenches to resemble those that Ukrainian troops actually encounter. The training trenches are "constructed by the Ukrainians, or they have told us how to construct it" to resemble the real ones as much as possible, Molde said.

He said the trench network has been "changed a couple of times already, and we've only been active for less than a year," highlighting the challenge of keeping up with a fast-evolving battlefield.

Though less of a focus for many Western militaries, trench operations are a critical and deadly part of regular operations, so it's a priority at Jomsborg. He said the goal is for as many Ukrainians to "survive this fight for as long as possible."

The hope, he added, is that "we reach a situation where Ukraine can negotiate a truce or a ceasefire on good terms. That's what it's all about."

title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
description: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa decides this week whether to ban Russian-language content in music and literature in public.
fullText:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

"The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy.

"With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."

But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov.

"Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.

Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk.

Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.

But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.

Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.

Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee.

"This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.

Barsky has been able to continue to perform in Russian because it is a private theatre.

The new language proposal - similar to one already in force in the capital Kyiv and some other cities – would urge but not require private premises including shops and cafes to adopt the ban.

Odesa's state-appointed language ombudswoman, Anna Nerush, who inspects premises to check on alleged violations of the rules, thinks if passed it will put pressure on them to comply.

"All businesses interact in one way or another with local government," she told the BBC. "They rent premises, they need advertising permits, and so on. So for many entities it's important to comply with a council decision, even if doesn't provide for sanctions for non-compliance. "

Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.

Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.

Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside.

"But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.

Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.

A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists.

"We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."

Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage.

"In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said.

"Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"

It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.

Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.

One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world.

Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.

Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian."

"Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."

You can hear more about the language controversy in Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

title: Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were useful; no sign of breakthrough
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks on Saturday with two U.S. envoys seeking a deal to
fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks on Saturday with two U.S. envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.

The ‌aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Ushakov did not say what ‌these ideas were.

He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield, was confident of achieving its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict."

All ​these are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly in the course of the war, which has dragged on for more than four and a half years and has seen both sides intensify long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.

There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday.

"The talks ‌went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the ⁠Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail," Ushakov said.

"Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides."

Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted afterwards on X that it had been ⁠an "important peacemaking visit." He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.

In televised remarks at the start of the talks, Putin praised Trump's efforts to end the war. Trump suggested on Friday the U.S. had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war, but did not elaborate.

"Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his ​efforts ​to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict," ​Putin said.

He promised to ensure the safety of the U.S. negotiators. ‌Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.

Over the previous 10 days, Russia had pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.

Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in a bid to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.

A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war, ‌the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.

A source close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports ​emerged of the trip by Trump's envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.

"There is ​no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes ​securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region," the source told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports ‌from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of ​the year.

Western military analysts see such a possibility ​as remote, given Moscow's slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.

The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory ​of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan ‌to join NATO — was "unshakeable."

Since the last U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside ​the other's territory, while the war at sea has also escalated.

(Additional reporting by Marina Bobrova, Anton Kolodyazhnyy and Vladimir Soldatkin in Moscow, Darya Korsunskaya ​in London, Olena Harmash in Kyiv; Writing by Mark Trevelyan; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

title: A US Army commander says facing Ukrainian hunters helped his troops figure out how to use armor in a drone-heavy fight
description: Russia's war in Ukraine has demonstrated that tanks and armored vehicles are vulnerable to drone threats. Obsolescence, though, is up for debate.
fullText:
A US Army commander wrote an op-ed about his troops' recent training fight against Ukrainian forces.

While drones were a problem, he said soldiers adapted their techniques, especially with their armored vehicles.

Officials and experts have debated the vulnerability of armored vehicles against drones.

A US Army commander wrote in a new opinion article that a recent combat training exercise against Ukrainian soldiers showed that armor like infantry fighting vehicles and tanks can still survive and make a difference on battlefields swarming with drones, but troops have to be able to adapt, to flexibly change how they move, hide, and fight.

During the simulated battle, his troops saw how persistent drone surveillance exposed their movements and put their combat vehicles at risk. But the soldiers also learned and adapted, the commander said.

On Friday, Capt. Allan W. Watson, the commander of Blackhawk Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment, wrote an op-ed in Task and Purpose about an April exercise. The exercise, held at Hohenfels Training Area in Germany, pit Watson's soldiers against Hohenfels' dedicated opposition force, the 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, with support from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Force's 412 Regiment.

The Ukrainian unit, known as "Nemesis," brought real combat experience fighting with and against drones to the training, presenting a demanding test for American soldiers. Reconnaissance drones tracked their movements, and US forces didn't have the counter-drone capabilities they wanted, Watson wrote.

Watson's soldiers responded by changing how they used their armored vehicles. They hid their Bradleys in gullies and among the trees, leveraged the terrain to mask their maneuvers, avoided predictable routes that they knew the Ukrainian hunters expected them to try, and deliberately considered how the force looked to overhead drones.

"More than once," he wrote, "I found myself standing sideways in the turret of our Bradley, barking orders as our platoons traversed 40-degree slopes, finding new routes to an objective."

"The enemy still found us," Watson wrote in the op-ed. But "even with drone reconnaissance, the enemy had to use traditional ground reconnaissance and infiltration techniques. While a drone could identify us from above, only troops on the ground could exploit the information."

Throughout the fight, the US forces lost Bradleys and tanks, which Watson said was expected in a high-pressure event like this, an exercise meant to resemble a real armed conflict.

For Watson, those losses didn't condemn his armored assets to irrelevance; rather, the training exercise demonstrated that armor still provides tremendously valuable mobility, protection, and firepower as long as it is put to use with the drone threat in mind.

"Our armor did not make us more vulnerable," he wrote, "it made us mobile, protected, and dangerous."

Officials and top war watchers have debated the value of armored vehicles against drones and uncrewed systems since the beginning of the Ukraine war, as reports from the front and video footage of drones blowing up tanks and armor across the battlefield circulated online.

The asymmetric threat raised concerns that the proliferation of cheap drones, both surveillance and attack, had made heavy armor too vulnerable, making it less relevant for future fights.

Watson's account of his experiences paints a more complicated picture, acknowledging that uncrewed systems represent a growing threat to armored combat vehicles but emphasizing that the threat hasn't yet made them obsolete. The debate goes on.

title: Putin cites chance of peace deal, Zelenskiy says US negotiators to visit both countries
description: VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zel...
fullText:
VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said U.S. negotiators trying to broker a deal would ‌soon visit both Moscow and Kyiv.

Putin, speaking at an economic forum in Russia's far east, said a number of countries including the U.S. ‌and China were ready to support a peace settlement.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine," he said.

"We are grateful to everyone ​attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is."

In Kyiv, Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address that preliminary dates had been set for a visit by U.S. negotiators.

"We expect to see representatives of the U.S. president here in Kyiv," Zelenskiy said.

"There will be a meeting with them in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are expecting a meeting with them in the coming days. It is very important. It is important that America ‌continues to be active."

In Washington, U.S. President Donald Trump ⁠said he wanted to see an end to the war and losses sustained by both sides.

"I just want to see that end. I think we'll get it," Trump told GB News in an interview that aired on Thursday, a day ⁠after telling reporters he wanted a summit with Putin when the Kremlin leader is ready for a peace deal.

After 4-1/2 years of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, it is rare for either side to offer an upbeat assessment of peace prospects. They last met for U.S.-mediated talks in February.

Since then, with the U.S. ​distracted by ​the Iran war, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range air attacks deep ​inside the other's territory. Hostilities at sea have escalated sharply ‌with attacks by both sides on ports and commercial shipping, pushing up global grain prices.

U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded the effort to broker an agreement, were last in Moscow in January. They have yet to visit Kyiv.

Chicago wheat futures dropped by more than 2% on Putin's comments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier told reporters in Kyiv that he saw a "new dynamic" coming in peace efforts, with more active political and diplomatic engagement.

Neither side, however, gave reasons to expect progress.

On the contrary, the Kremlin leader said Ukraine's latest actions presented an obstacle.

In response to a question, Putin ‌said Ukrainian attacks on civilian merchant ships and "reported threats of attacks on civilian aircraft" ​were "acts of state terrorism", which he said "complicates the prospects for bilateral peace talks".

Zelenskiy warned airlines ​and insurance companies this week that the presence of Ukrainian drones had ​made Russian skies dangerous, although he said Ukraine would target only Russian military facilities and not threaten civilian aircraft.

On ‌Wednesday, Ukraine urged the U.N.'s aviation agency to ask members to ​ban operations in Russian airspace. Ukraine ​has been cut off from international civil aviation because its own airspace is considered unsafe since Russia invaded in 2022.

PUTIN: CONTACTS MOSTLY TAKE PLACE VIA INTELLIGENCE AGENCIES

Putin said contacts with Ukraine were still taking place.

"It is difficult for me to say right now to what extent these ​contacts are leading to a peace agreement, given ‌the statements we have heard recently from Ukraine's top leadership," he said.

"However, contacts do exist and are continuing on an ongoing basis - ​gain, primarily through intelligence channels."

(Additional reporting by Reuters in Moscow, Max Hunder in Kyiv, Anna Pruchnicka in Gdansk and Tabahriti, Sam ​in London); Writing by Mark Trevelyan; Editing by Andrew Heavens and David Gregorio)

title: Ukraine's drone attacks caused turmoil for Russians throughout summer
description: Online orders were disrupted as e-commerce hubs were set ablaze by buzzing drones.  It's been a difficult summer for Russians — a season of almost daily turmoil, frustration and anxiety.  The war that...
fullText:
There were long lines at gas pumps, turning each fill-up into an ordeal. Flights to vacation destinations were canceled, delayed or rerouted. Online orders were disrupted as e-commerce hubs were set ablaze by buzzing drones.

It's been a difficult summer for Russians — a season of almost daily turmoil, frustration and anxiety.

The war that President Vladimir Putin unleashed on Ukraine 4½ years ago has come home and is harder to ignore. Nightly swarms of drones closed Russian airports, struck oil refineries or set ablaze the warehouses of retail giants Wildberries and Ozon.

Over 43,300 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over Russia and illegally annexed Crimea in June, July and August, according to Defense Ministry data compiled by The Associated Press, although some clearly hit their targets. In the same period last summer, about 7,700 were intercepted, the ministry said.

"We were living a normal life, and then suddenly it's like this," retiree Margarita Terekhova said about waiting in line to refuel her car in Moscow, part of the nationwide gas crisis from refinery attacks that persisted into August.

As the calendar turns toward autumn, increased awareness of the war and its consequences comes at a challenging time for the Kremlin. A parliamentary election takes place Sept. 18-20 — the first since the full-scale invasion.

While there's little doubt about the outcome of the tightly controlled balloting that features few opposition candidates, analysts say it still holds potential for political volatility.

"Elections are a time when people should reflect on themselves, the country, where it's going and what to do about it," said Nikolay Petrov, senior research fellow at the NEST Centre, founded by exiled tycoon and opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.

Even in a strictly controlled environment, "things that are unexpected, inconvenient (and) painful for the authorities" can happen, Petrov said.

The summer's first major attack came June 3, when an oil terminal outside St. Petersburg was struck just as Putin's signature economic forum there got underway. Since then, Ukraine hit refineries, along with Wildberries and Ozon warehouses — from Moscow to Yekaterinburg in the Ural Mountains, to Omsk in Siberia.

That intensified campaign — with its expanded geography and a growing number of drones — shocked Russians, says Denis Volkov, director of the country's top independent pollster, the Levada Center.

Ukraine has not disclosed how many drones it launches, but President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has talked about expanding the strikes, which he calls "long-range sanctions." Officials in Kyiv say they will continue trying to pressure Russia into ending the war, even as Moscow intensifies its bombardment of Ukraine.

The attacks have remained the most noteworthy topic for two months this summer, Volkov told AP.

Social media documented gas station queues or travelers stranded by canceled flights. Tearful entrepreneurs told followers their inventory was destroyed at the stricken warehouses.

Asked if Russians should get used to fuel shortages, Putin said Thursday in Vladivostok that "we must be prepared for anything, and our preparedness for everything will signal to those who want to harm us that it's better not to do it."

While the shock over this summer's events has since eased, Volkov said, there is a longer-term downward trend that sociologists have tracked since last year: a worsening assessment of Russia's economic situation and declining approvals of top politicians.

Putin's traditionally high approval rating has fallen somewhat this year. Data from the Levada Center showed it at 76% in August, down from 87% in September 2025.

Chris Weafer, CEO of the Macro-Advisory Ltd. consultancy that works in Moscow, said there's more awareness of the war and less complacency about it.

"People are grumbling more, they're talking more," he said, with a striking level of pessimism, especially in the business community, about the prospects for its end.

There also appears to be nervousness fueled by persistent rumors of an impending troop mobilization — like the widely unpopular one in September 2022 that drafted 300,000 men.

Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials maintain Russia is planning another mobilization after the State Duma election. Putin rejected the claims, saying they were "an information attack by the enemy."

Still, the prospect has prompted some Russians to leave the country. One 23-year-old Muscovite told AP she left last month with her husband, worried he might be drafted.

The young woman, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of concerns for her safety, also mentioned fear of Ukrainian attacks. She believes many feel exhaustion from the war, which now can affect "the life of any person in any corner of the country," she said.

Volkov said worries over a new mobilization have long lurked in the background but flared up slightly last year after U.S.-led peace efforts stalled with no end to the war in sight.

People "don't want (the conflict) to expand and more people to be dragged into it against their will, and this breeds certain concern, anxiety," he said.

Volkov and Weafer said this increased awareness and the dampened mood aren't translating into anti-war demonstrations, public unrest or even enough protest votes to affect the balloting.

But things like turnout and "debate ahead of the election" still matter to authorities, Weafer said, even with an all-but-certain outcome.

Petrov pointed to the Yabloko party, the longtime voice of the liberal opposition that campaigns for an end to the war. It initially was allowed onto the ballot, and its young supporters flooded social media with videos promoting the party.

But on Aug. 10, the Supreme Court kicked Yabloko off the ballot, leaving it to compete only in single constituency races. Ten days later, the head of its Moscow office, Kirill Goncharov, said the party, with about 4,000 members, got 8,000 new applications.

"The context of the summer of 2026 is that there is a demand for peace," Goncharov said.

Yabloko's slogans resonated with young voters, and that "upended the Kremlin's calculation" of giving people a relatively safe outlet for their discontent, Petrov said.

Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center said Yabloko's removal showed that authorities did not want the election to become a debate "for and against peace."

Petrov said the Kremlin needs elections "as a demonstration of its great legitimacy." It doesn't care so much about the results, since it largely controls all the parties.

"Elections, like in Soviet times, should demonstrate the complete loyalty of all citizens," he said, adding that the vote should signal that Putin and the Kremlin have everything under control, and that people are ready to do "whatever authorities ask of them."

Russians interviewed in Moscow this week about how they spent their summer recounted contented moments, but they also described living with the effects of daily drone attacks.

Natalya Bazhenova from Chita in Siberia told AP she waited two full days in line for gasoline. Visiting the Voronezh region near the Ukrainian border, she got constant texts warning of drones but heard no explosions.

Ksenia Smirnova said her family canceled a flight to a Black Sea resort and is going by train instead.

On Tuesday, Zelenskyy ominously warned airlines in Russia that the risks could continue.

title: Russian general accused of masterminding the attack against Kyiv’s children’s hospital injured in assassination attempt
description: A Russian general who has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against a children’s hospital in Kyiv has reportedly been shot in northwestern Russia on Thursday.
fullText:
A Russian general who has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against a children's hospital in Kyiv has reportedly been shot in northwestern Russia on Thursday.

The Russian Investigative Committee said it opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a military service member who was shot several times in the city of Engels in the Saratov region on Thursday.

While the committee did not name the man, Russian telegram channels widely reported it was Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, the commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of the Russian Aerospace Forces' Long-Range Aviation.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later alluded to the attack in his daily address, saying "we will also carry out our own asymmetric operations in response" to Russia.

"The Russian criminals did not hide - they will be found. And today brings another confirmation of this fact, a confirmation in the Saratov region," he added.

Engels serves as the home base of Russia's strategic bombers fleet, including the Tu-95MS and Tu-160 aircraft that Moscow uses to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.

Varpakhovich has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against Kyiv's Okhmatdyt hospital in July 2024.

The attack killed three people – one of them a child who was wounded in the strike and died a few days later – and injured dozens others. Several of the hospital's departments, including the intensive care units, the oncology and surgical wings, the toxicology and trauma center, were damaged or destroyed.

The hospital said afterwards that hundreds of patients and staff were evacuated when the air raid alarm was raised indicating an incoming an strike. But some, including three patients undergoing a heart surgery, were still there when the missile hit about an hour later.

Varpakhovich has also been sanctioned by multiple countries and the European Union over his role in the 2024

While Ukraine has not commented on the incident, Varpakhovych has recently been on Kyiv's radar.

The Security Service of Ukraine and the country's Prosecutor General formally charged him with war crimes three days ago, saying he ordered the long-range aviation units under his command to launch a Kh-101 air-to-ground cruise missile against the hospital.

The Russian investigative committee said the serviceman survived the attack and was transported to a hospital. Local media reported that he was flown to Moscow for treatment after being shot in the face and the torso.

Varpakhovich is the latest of high-profile military officials targeted in apparent assassinations in Russia over the past few years. Moscow has pointed finger at Ukraine over these killings, but Kyiv has never officially acknowledged playing a role in any of them.

Igor Kirillov, a general in charge of the Russian military's nuclear and chemical weapons protection forces, was killed in December 2024 when an explosive device planted on a scooter was detonated near him.

Lt. Gen. Yaroslav Moskalik, deputy head of the main operational department of the General Staff and Lt. Gen. Fanil Sarvarov, who ran the armed forces operational training department, were both killed in car explosions in Moscow last year.

Others who have been killed include the founder of a pro-Russian militia group, Armen Sarkisyan, described by Ukraine as a "criminal mastermind," who died following a bombing in central Moscow, in February 2025.

title: Norway seizes Russian vessel to enforce $4.22B Ukrainian arbitration claim

fullText:
OSLO, Norway (AP) — Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard on Wednesday at the request of Ukraine's Naftogaz as part of a global effort to enforce a $4.22 billion arbitration award.

Naftogaz is trying to recover the multibillion-dollar arbitration award stemming from Russia's 2014 illegal annexation of Crimea and its seizure of Ukrainian energy assets, including gas fields and pipelines.

In 2023, an arbitration tribunal in The Hague ordered Russia to pay the $4.22 billion to the Ukrainian state-owned energy company for unlawfully seizing its assets in Crimea.

After Russia's refusal to pay the award, Naftogaz has been petitioning national courts seeking court orders to seize Russian commercial assets.

"This is another important step towards restoring justice for Russia's unlawful seizure of Naftogaz assets in Crimea. Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award. We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world," said Naftogaz CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

When asked on Thursday about Norway's action, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the seizure of civilian vessels and strikes on merchant shipping were "acts of state terrorism."

He also condemned recent warnings by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to foreign airlines that flying in Russia would no longer be safe because of Ukrainian long-range drone attacks.

Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Russia, Putin linked the vessel seizure and Zelenskyy's warning, saying such incidents "complicated" the prospects for future peace talks. He added that Ukraine's allies were "complicit in international terrorism" by remaining silent on the issues.

Norway's seizure of the Russian vessel, the Professor Molchanov, comes after a Nord-Troms district court order issued August 31, Svalbard Governor Lars Fause said in a statement.

Following the seizure, the vessel is not allowed to leave its current location in Barentsburg on Svalbard, the governor said.

The Russian vessel is used for commercial expedition cruises, including to Svalbard.

title: Ukrainian soldiers are finding deceptive uses for their unjammable fiber-optic drones as ambush tactics spread
description: Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in to study Russian bunkers and also shape attacks, a soldier said.
fullText:
Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in deceptive new ways, a soldier said.

They can gather close-up intel on Russian bunkers and help shape attacks.

Drones that wait to strike are becoming a growing battlefield threat.

Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in increasingly deceptive ways, relying on their resistance to electronic warfare and close-range video feeds to scout Russian positions, study bunkers and dugouts, and create unusual openings for attacks, a soldier said.

These jamming-resistant drones have been on the battlefield for over two years, and they have become an important tool for both sides, allowing troops to surveil and attack without their drones being brought down by electronic warfare.

Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now an analyst in Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that Ukrainian operators are increasingly using fiber-optic drones in atypical ways — such as deception and ambush — to "create tons of chaos."

He said that some operators have their drones play dead or purposefully lie in wait on the battlefield, exploding at just the right time to kill an approaching soldier or expose a protected enemy position rather than simply flying directly into a target and detonating on impact.

He said fiber-optic drones are also helpful for studying Russian bunkers and dugouts because they can capture high-quality video of "all of the entrances, because you get the perfect footage, you could literally figure out what type of cover that they have on their entry to their dugout, and what you should do to open it."

Close-range reconnaissance is one of the drone's best uses, Zhluktenko said. Before hitting Russian dugouts and bunkers, drone operators can gather "very good intel" and "very precise intelligence at very, very close range."

While they can be used to chase and attack, he said, there are limitations that make them less than ideal for those missions. These drones, which are connected to the operator by a thin data cable, are slower than the untethered FPV drones, and the fiber-optic cables can "break quite easily when you just give it a full throttle."

For fiber-optic drones, pilot commands and video feeds are transmitted through a physical cable instead of over radio frequency connections, which can be jammed by electronic warfare. The cable is delicate and can snap if caught on trees or obstacles. Some soldiers carry scissors to cut through any cables they come across.

A US veteran who has fought for Ukraine told Business Insider on the condition of anonymity that there are "very simple ways to bring them down," including by cutting their wires.

"In the wintertime," he said, "the cold will break them half the time." Still, these systems are considered necessary given the prolific electronic warfare threat.

Zhluktenko said the cable was becoming more expensive, which has limited how often the drones are used. He said Ukraine was finding other ways to try to get the same stable connection, including by using masses of signal repeaters to keep radio connections online, but fiber-optic drones remain in play.

The deception and ambush tactics Zhluktenko described are part of a growing trend on both sides of this war.

A British medic working in Ukraine who spoke to Business Insider on the condition of anonymity said that Russia places drones in positions for ambushes.

Russian drones, she said, will "actually sit within the grass or the verges, and a group of soldiers will either go past or drive past, and these things will literally activate and just almost jump out of nowhere and hit. "

"We have this image of drones flying, making a great noise and making a great presence, but that is not the case," she said. "They can be quiet, insidious, and the one minute you'll be, shall I say, walking along a tree line, the next thing, you hear the noise, and then we see an explosion, and it's just so incredibly rapid. And because they're so fast, it's often way beyond your reflexes to actually react."

Another US veteran who fought in Ukraine told Business Insider that Russian soldiers will use "land mine tactics," where they put the drone next to a road and leave it there, waiting for a vehicle or another target to approach.

Ukrainians have called attention to these tactics as well. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, then serving as a drone warfare advisor to Ukraine's defense ministry, said last year that Russia was using fiber-optic drones for "ambush" tactics, including lying in wait for targets along roadways.

"This is one of the tactics involving fiber-optic drones," he said. "It's effective and causes us a lot of problems." Russia is also using solar-powered drones that can lie dormant for this tactic.

"The drones hide on roads and at intersections," Beskrestnov said. "They're often placed on forest trails, waiting for a target. When they spot a vehicle, they take off and strike quickly, leaving little time to react."

title: FIA wrong to lift Russia ban - Ukraine minister

fullText:
Motorsport's governing body the FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors because nothing has changed since it was imposed, the Ukrainian Minister for Youth and Sport says.

Matvii Bidnyi said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

Bidnyi said that the central rail station in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv had been bombed by a Russian drone on Wednesday just an hour before he spoke to BBC Sport.

"The air alert was just turning off," Bidnyi said. "Our kids, we all came from the bomb shelter. These attacks continue almost every day.

"Russia continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Belarus can continue to provide military support to Russia. Ukrainian people are still being killed every day. And Russian attacks become more and more brutal.

"I don't understand, and Ukrainian people, and I know that all European people don't understand what's happened, why now we must to make this policy softer."

Russian Athletics files new claim against sanctions

Russia could compete at LA 2028 Olympics

The ban on Russian and Belarussian competitors taking part in international motorsport events was imposed in February 2022, after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine.

It was lifted on 3 August this year in a decision by the FIA's world motorsport council. This followed the International Olympic Association, with which the FIA is affiliated, lifting its own ban.

Bidnyi pointed out that other sports organisations had not followed this route, including World Athletics.

"When any federation lifts the ban and makes steps towards the aggressor, the terrorist state, it's always really, really sad," he said.

"It's a massive disappointment for everyone in Ukraine. And we think it undermines the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor.

"Unfortunately, there are a lot of international sports organisations trying to lift bans to release pressure from the aggressor. We can observe it in such a federation as judo, weightlifting, and then a lot of others.

"But we have strong partners and strong principle international organisations - for example, biathlon or athletics - who understand the responsibility of the international sports community for international order and justice."

The Russian Athletics Federation has filed a claim with the Court of Arbitration for Sport to challenge the sanctions imposed by World Athletics.

Bidnyi said: "In Russia, elite sport is deeply connected with the military and state propaganda system. It's one of the biggest whitewashing mechanisms. This is why we call it sportswashing."

The Ukraine government says that the war "has had a devastating impact on Ukrainian sport as a whole - since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion: 775 Ukrainian athletes and coaches have been killed by Russia", including three competitors in the Ukrainian Automobile Federation.

It says Russia "has made sport facilities their targets to continue killing - more than 925 sports facilities have been destroyed".

The FIA was contacted for comment. Last week, it issued a statement regarding the decision to lift the ban on Russian competitors.

A spokesperson said: "The FIA has updated the requirements for Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, competitors and officials following a vote by the world motorsport council. This follows an announcement by the IOC on 7th July and similar updates issued by other international sporting federations.

"The FIA maintains its ban on organising events and competitions in Russia and Belarus. The FIA continues to monitor the situation closely in Ukraine and reserves the right to update its position in the future."

MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russia was winning the war in Ukraine and portrayed the Ukrainian leadership as "terrorists" with whom Moscow could not negotiate.

Putin, in his most detailed ‌comments on the war for many weeks, acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks inside Russia had inflicted real damage and said that drones ‌posed a particular challenge.

But he said that Russia was advancing on the battlefield and told reporters: "I have no doubt the enemy will crumble."

He declined to say when that ​would happen.

Rumours that Russia would be forced to order a new military mobilisation were "utter nonsense," he said.

PUTIN SAYS RUSSIAN ADVANCES ARE ACCELERATING

Four and a half years into the war, Russia controls about a fifth of Ukraine. U.S.-mediated peace talks broke off in February after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran.

Opinion polls suggest growing war fatigue in Russia and influential voices are warning about the strain on its economy.

But Putin struck ‌a confident, hawkish tone as he rattled through ⁠a detailed version of developments on the front line, saying Russian advances were accelerating.

Russian troops had captured 270 square km (104 sq miles) of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine in August and two large groups of Ukrainian ⁠troops - one comprising 4,500 to 4,800 men, the other up to 2,000 - were surrounded, he said. Reuters could not independently verify those assertions.

Russia continues to advance towards the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Putin said, adding that Moscow's forces were preparing to launch massive strikes against energy infrastructure in Ukraine.

Putin said ​that ​Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's warning to airlines that Ukrainian drones would effectively shut ​down Russian airspace sounded like "state terrorism" and that Moscow ‌would find a way to respond if it happened.

Speaking at a news conference after a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said it was not possible to negotiate with "terrorists".

He also said, however, that Moscow was open to talks aimed at ending, rather than freezing, the war, and restated its willingness to talk to U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys.

"If someone makes, or can make, a tangible contribution to this process, we are all in favour," Putin said.

"The only thing we would want to avoid is the process spinning its wheels pointlessly. However, if someone is capable of bringing ‌something positive to these negotiations - which, as we understand it, are currently somewhat ​frozen - then, generally speaking, we are not opposed."

Putin specifically acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes ​had caused damage to Russian oil refineries, although without referring ​to widespread fuel shortages that have resulted from those attacks.

But he said that the level of protection had ‌improved, and "we only have 10% of our refineries left to ​repair".

Putin responded scathingly to an accusation ​by the German government on Tuesday that Russia was to blame for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.

He said the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz was pointing the finger at Moscow to distract from domestic problems and falling approval ratings.

Putin ​accused Germany of planting evidence in order to ‌frame Russia for the drone attack, but he did not say what he was basing that accusation on.

title: Ukraine dissects Russia’s Zircon missile as Moscow leans on harder-to-intercept weapons
description: A Ukrainian official says Russia's growing use of harder-to-intercept missiles marks a dangerous new stage as Patriot interceptor stocks run low.
fullText:
Ukraine's military intelligence published a detailed breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile.

The assessment reveals its components, speed, manufacturers, and foreign-made parts.

Russia has leaned more on hard-to-intercept missiles as Ukraine has gotten better at stopping other threats.

Ukraine's main military intelligence agency published a breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile, a weapon Moscow has increasingly employed in its intensifying strikes.

Russia has been investing heavily in advancing its missile arsenal, upgrading systems and making them harder for air defenses to intercept. That reaction to Ukrainian air-defense wins now represents a major challenge as interceptors run low.

On Monday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, shared details on Russia's 3M22 Zircon missile, including its components and production.

It also provided details on the main manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyeniya, a Russian defense company that is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation, and foreign parts used in the weapon, which included some made by US companies. The disclosure also named more than 70 companies and dozens of people involved in its production.

In its new assessment, the GUR referred to Zircon as a ballistic missile, a departure from Russia's description of it as a hypersonic cruise missile. New details published by Ukraine describe it as a two-stage ballistic missile featuring a solid-fuel booster and a solid-fuel sustainer for flight.

Cruise missiles and ballistic missiles differ in how they fly and reach their targets. Ballistic missiles typically climb on a ballistic trajectory before descending at high speed toward their targets, while cruise missiles are jet-propelled and fly lower within the atmosphere.

Ukraine's assessment challenges Russia's long-standing characterization of the weapon.

The GUR also assessed that the Zircon is slower than claimed, with a maximum speed of Mach 6.8. Russia claims that the missile can reach speeds of Mach 9.

Russia has previously touted the Zircon missile as one of its "invincible" hypersonic weapons. It first used the missile against Ukraine in February 2024. At that time, Ukraine estimated that Russia had around 40 stockpiled.

The arsenal has since grown, though estimates vary, and Russia has increasingly fired these missiles in strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, leaning harder on more advanced missiles as Ukraine has demonstrated it can intercept other Russian systems.

"Since we learned to shoot down more than 90% of cruise missiles and drones with gasoline piston engines, Russia has decided to rely on ballistics and jet drones," Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider.

Russia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comment on Ukrainian assessments of its weapons and motives.

Cherniev said that Ukraine assesses that Russia has reduced production of Kinzhal missiles because of accuracy issues and instead focused on producing Iskander and Zircon missiles. Russian forces have ramped up ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year, including debuting a new upgraded variant of its Iskander series, the Iskander-1000, earlier this summer.

These ballistic missiles are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept, and Russia's growing reliance on them comes as Ukraine struggles with shortages of critical air-defense interceptors. Ukraine relies on the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system to confront Russia's more difficult missiles, but it has warned that interceptor stocks are running low.

"This is a new and extremely dangerous stage of the war, which requires us to be more effective in the fight against high-speed jet drones, as well as additional assistance from the United States in the form of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems," Cherniev said.
